In the creche on the ground floor of a Mumbai housing society, Gargi, five, snatched the red tricycle from little Tuhin. He sat down hard and wailed.
Neelam aunty, who ran the creche, didn't scold. She crouched beside Gargi and took out a set of face cards. "Which face is Tuhin making?"

Since her father, Vikas, had stopped leaving for the office in the mornings, Sunaina, ten, had stopped asking about it. When a friend in the Andheri building lift asked why he was home so much, Sunaina said, "He's working from home. We're fine," and stared at the floor numbers.
At dinner Vikas began, "Sunu, you know the company—"
"I have maths homework," she said, and carried her plate to her room.
She lay awake past midnight watching the ceiling fan turn. Next morning she snapped at her little brother for using her pencil, then cried in the bathroom without knowing why.
At breakfast Vikas saw her red eyes and rested a hand on her shoulder. "After school, just us two. We'll talk."

qa.q: What reason did Sunaina give her friend for Vikas being home?
qa.a: She said he's working from home.

qa.q: Why does Sunaina escape to her room when Vikas starts to explain?
qa.a: Not hearing the details seems safer to her than facing the worry about her father's job, so homework becomes a way out.

qa.q: What choice did Vikas make at breakfast, and why might it help?
qa.a: He offered a private talk after school, giving Sunaina a safe, set time to hear the news gently instead of dodging it.

qa.q: How might Sunaina's little brother experience her snapping?
qa.a: He probably feels confused and hurt, since he only used a pencil and doesn't know the worry behind her temper.

grounding: A ten-year-old whose father has stopped going to work insists all is well and avoids the talk, while poor sleep and snapping show the strain.

"Uma, can we talk about my job?" Jaya asked, sitting on the edge of her daughter's bed.
"It's fine, Amma. I know. It's fine."
"The office closed my team. I'm looking for—"
"I said it's fine! Can you switch off the light?"
Jaya switched it off but didn't leave. "You've been awake late every night this week."
Silence. Then, very small: "Are we going to have to move?"
"Not now. And if anything changes, you'll hear it from me first."
"Okay." A long pause. "Sorry I shouted at Nikhil about the remote."
"I know, kanna. Worry makes everyone snappy. Me too."

qa.q: What happened to Jaya's team at the office?
qa.a: The office closed it.

qa.q: Why does Uma keep repeating 'It's fine'?
qa.a: Saying it's fine lets Uma avoid the details, which feel scarier than not knowing, even though the worry keeps her awake.

qa.q: Which of Jaya's choices opened the way to Uma's real question?
qa.a: Jaya switched off the light but stayed, and gently named the late nights, giving Uma room to ask about moving.

qa.q: How does Jaya seem to feel about Uma shouting at Nikhil?
qa.a: Jaya isn't angry; she understands that worry makes everyone snappy and admits she feels it too.

grounding: A girl whose mother has lost her job keeps saying it is fine and avoids the talk, while late nights and shouting show the strain.

This happened the winter I was eleven. Papa's shop closed, and I decided the best thing was not to ask. If anyone mentioned it, I said, "We're fine." I said it so often I almost believed it.
But I kept waking at three in the morning with my heart thumping. At school, when my friend Imran borrowed my eraser without asking, I yelled at him in front of everyone. He looked at me as if I were a stranger.
That evening I finally asked Papa, "Is it bad?" He told me the truth, in small pieces. It was hard to hear. But after that, I slept.
— Usha

qa.q: At what time did Usha keep waking up?
qa.a: At three in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Usha decide the best thing was not to ask?
qa.a: Not knowing felt safer than hearing bad news about Papa's shop, so saying "We're fine" kept the fear at arm's length.

qa.q: What turning point helped Usha sleep again?
qa.a: Finally asking Papa "Is it bad?" and hearing the truth in small pieces; facing it eased the worry that had been leaking out.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt being yelled at over an eraser?
qa.a: Imran was probably shocked and hurt, since the anger was far bigger than a borrowed eraser and he couldn't know about the shop.

grounding: A child looks back on insisting all was fine after Papa's shop closed, while waking at night and yelling at a friend showed the worry.

Counsellor's note: Hafsa, Class 11
Hafsa's chemistry unit test came back at 11 out of 40. For a week she told classmates the papers "hadn't been checked properly" and didn't unfold hers.
Today she came to my room. She sat for a while, then said, "I got 11. That's my mark." She let herself be upset, and I didn't rush it.
Once she had said it aloud, we could talk. She picked two chapters to redo first and decided to show her teacher her corrections on Friday. She also plans to tell her mother tonight, with me there if she wants.
Follow-up next Wednesday.
— Nitin

qa.q: What mark did Hafsa get in her chemistry unit test?
qa.a: 11 out of 40.

qa.q: Why might Hafsa have said the papers hadn't been checked properly?
qa.a: Blaming the checking softened the shock, letting her put off the feeling of having done badly for a while.

qa.q: What choice helped Hafsa move from denial to action?
qa.a: Saying the mark aloud to one trusted person first, then choosing just two chapters and a day to show her corrections.

qa.q: How might Hafsa's chemistry teacher see the corrections on Friday?
qa.a: The teacher will likely see a student who faced a low mark and is working on it, which is far easier to help than someone avoiding the paper.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenager moving from denying a low mark to saying it aloud to one person and then planning small steps.

Tuesday night
Okay. Writing it here so it's real. I failed the maths prelim. 23 out of 80.
All afternoon I told myself the answer key must be wrong. I didn't even look at where I'd lost marks. Then Seema Masi called to ask how school was, and I don't know why, but I just said it. "Masi, I failed maths."
She didn't gasp. She said, "Okay. Thank you for telling me. Which chapter do you want to look at first?"
So I looked. Most of it was trigonometry. I made a list of three things for this week.
Still feel sick. But less.
— Leela

qa.a: Most of it was trigonometry.

qa.a: Saying "I failed maths" aloud to Seema Masi; once one trusted person knew, looking at the paper and making a list became possible.

qa.a: Seema Masi probably wanted Leela to feel safe after saying it, knowing a shocked reaction could send Leela back to avoiding the paper.

passage:
Looking back at second year, I can see exactly what I was doing. My marks in two papers dropped, and the hostel fee reminder came three times. Each time I thought, "It'll sort itself out. Something will turn up." When the student counsellor emailed, I archived it without opening it. Not looking felt strangely calm.
My roommate Divyansh asked once whether I'd paid the fee. I changed the subject to the cricket match.
Then the notice went up: fees unpaid by Friday meant no hall ticket. My stomach dropped. On Thursday I finally opened that email, sat in the counsellor's office, and learnt about an instalment option I could have known about weeks earlier.
— Binita

qa.q: What did Binita do with the counsellor's email?
qa.a: Archived it without opening it.

qa.q: Why did not looking feel strangely calm to Binita?
qa.a: Avoiding the email and reminders kept the dread at a distance, so it felt calmer than facing falling marks and an unpaid fee.

qa.q: What could Binita have done at the first fee reminder instead?
qa.a: Opening the counsellor's email or asking the office straight away could have turned up the instalment option weeks earlier, with far less panic.

qa.q: What might Divyansh have sensed when Binita changed the subject?
qa.a: Divyansh may have sensed something was wrong with the fee and felt unsure whether to push or let it go.

grounding: A student looks back on dodging falling marks, fee reminders and the counsellor's email until a hall-ticket deadline forced action.

Student support note: Pallavi, B.Com second year
I emailed Pallavi on 3 and 17 September after her attendance and internal marks dropped. No reply. A friend of hers told me Pallavi kept saying, "It'll sort itself out, I'm just tired."
On 1 October the accounts office flagged unpaid fees; exam registration closes on the 10th. Today, the 8th, Pallavi came in holding the office printout. She said she had seen my emails in her inbox and couldn't make herself click them.
I didn't lecture. We made three calls together: the accounts office, her class mentor, and her father. By the end she was breathing more easily.
Next: weekly check-in on Mondays.
— Himani

qa.q: When did the accounts office flag Pallavi's unpaid fees?
qa.a: On 1 October.

qa.q: Why couldn't Pallavi make herself click the emails?
qa.a: Opening them would have made the falling marks and fees real, and not looking kept the dread down until the deadline came close.

qa.q: What choice by Himani helped once Pallavi came in?
qa.a: Himani skipped the lecture and made the three calls alongside her, turning a frightening pile into a few concrete steps.

qa.q: How might Pallavi's friend have felt hearing 'It'll sort itself out'?
qa.a: The friend may have been worried but unsure what to do, sensing that things weren't really fine.

grounding: A support officer's note records a student ignoring falling marks, unpaid fees and emails until the registration deadline brought her in.
